name: Scoliosis bracing / fusion surgery

lead: Scoliosis bracing and spinal fusion are medical treatments for sideways spinal curvature. Results include a straighter, more symmetrical back and torso, and Wikipedia notes visible changes can affect teenagers' quality of life and cosmetic concerns are a key reason adults choose surgery.

The chain is a curve halted or surgically straightened, a more symmetrical spine, then a straighter, more even torso. Bracing is used in growing patients to stop a curve worsening, with evidence that it prevents progression; its effect on appearance, quality of life or back pain is unclear. Fusion is generally reserved for curves projected to pass about 45 to 50 degrees.

paras: For growing patients, curves under 20 degrees are monitored, 20 to 29 degrees are managed by risk factors, and curves over 30 degrees generally prompt a bracing recommendation. A rigid torso brace such as the Boston brace is typically worn 22 to 23 hours a day. Fusion joins vertebrae with metal instrumentation and bone graft to correct and hold the curve.

Surgery is major, can be painful and has a months-long recovery, and full straightening is usually not possible. Brace effectiveness depends on how consistently it is worn, and braces have caused skin irritation and low self-esteem.

social.title: Doctors Getting Rich With Fusion Surgery Debunked by Studies

angle.text: Bracing in growing teens and spinal fusion for severe curves are established orthopaedic treatments that stop or correct spinal curvature, giving a straighter, more symmetrical back and torso. Cosmetic concerns are one reason adults choose surgery.

lead: Bracing and spinal fusion are the two main treatments for progressive scoliosis. Bracing is used only while a patient is still growing, aiming to stop the curve progressing to the point where surgery is needed.[1] Surgery is usually recommended for curves likely to progress beyond about 45 to 50 degrees, for curves interfering with breathing or sitting, and for curves that would be cosmetically unacceptable in adulthood.[1]

For growing patients, curves under 20 degrees are monitored, 20 to 29 degrees are managed according to risk factors, and curves over 30 degrees generally prompt a bracing recommendation.[1] The most common brace is the thoracolumbar sacral orthosis such as the Boston brace, typically worn 22 to 23 hours a day.[1]
Wikipedia states that evidence shows bracing prevents curve progression, while its effect on quality of life, appearance or back pain is unclear.[1]
infobox: Growing patients, curves about 30 to 45 degrees[1]

paras: Bracing criteria from the Scoliosis Research Society include curves progressing past 25 degrees, curves between 30 and 45 degrees, Risser sign 0 to 2, and under six months since menarche.[1] Night-only braces are more convenient but their effectiveness is uncertain.[1] The early Milwaukee brace, with metal rods attached to a girdle, was associated with jaw and muscle pain, skin irritation and low self-esteem.[1] A Scoliosis Research Society committee published standardised criteria for brace studies in 2005 after finding inconsistent inclusion criteria and effectiveness definitions in prior literature.[2]

A prospective study using a temperature sensor embedded in a Wilmington brace related objectively measured wear time to curve progression.[3] An electronic monitor called the Cricket was evaluated for tracking brace wear.[4] Research has examined how brace visual aesthetics affect acceptance and compliance, patients' preferences for brace treatment, and psychosocial predictors of non-wear in adolescents.[5][6][7]

Surgery uses anterior fusion through the chest wall, posterior fusion through the back with metal instrumentation, or both, and may take four to eight hours.[1] Return to physical activity takes around six months, and full straightening is usually not possible although significant correction is typical.[1] Paul Harrington introduced a ratcheted rod system in 1962; two-rod systems followed in the 1970s and Cotrel-Dubousset instrumentation in the 1980s.[1] Wikipedia reports the average US hospital cost of surgical cases at about $30,000 to $60,000 per person in 2010.[1]

Studies listed above examine brace compliance and design. Registered trials include a randomised trial of a flexible thoracolumbar brace, trials of new or 3D-printed braces and a brace-treatment prevention trial of 170 participants.[8][9][10] Some studies examine pain management with a brace in adults.[11] Most registered trials concern brace design and monitoring; outcomes for non-medical appearance goals are not the focus.

Wikipedia notes that visible changes can significantly affect teenagers' quality of life and in extreme cases cause emotional stress, and that cosmetic concerns are a key reason adults pursue surgery.[1]

timeline.event: Paul Harrington introduces a ratcheted metal rod system.[1]
